technical.prompt: What is the four-party card model?

choices.answer: Cardholder, issuer, merchant and acquirer via a network
distractors: Four banks sharing one customer account
Four payment apps on a single phone
Four currencies used in one payment

technical.prompt: How does a three-party network differ from a four-party one?
expectedPoints: The network acts as both issuer and acquirer

choices.answer: The network issues cards and signs up merchants itself
distractors: It uses three currencies instead of four
It requires three banks for each payment
It only works for cash payments

technical.prompt: What are the three main stages of a card payment?

choices.answer: Authorisation, clearing and settlement

technical.prompt: What is the merchant discount rate?
expectedPoints: Total fee a merchant pays to accept cards
Covers interchange, network fees and acquirer margin

choices.answer: The total fee a merchant pays per card sale
distractors: A discount shoppers get for paying cash
The rate merchants pay on their loans
A sales tax on retail purchases

technical.prompt: What is interchange-plus-plus pricing?
expectedPoints: Merchant pays interchange + scheme fees + acquirer markup

choices.answer: Passing through interchange and scheme fees, plus a separate markup
distractors: A single flat rate for every card
A price that includes no interchange

technical.prompt: What is blended or flat-rate pricing?

choices.answer: A single simple rate charged for every card type
distractors: A different rate for every single card
Pricing that includes no fees at all
A rate set by the government

technical.prompt: What is the difference between card-present and card-not-present payments?

choices.answer: Card-present uses a physical card; CNP is online or by phone
distractors: Card-not-present uses a physical card at a till
Both carry exactly the same fraud risk
Card-present applies only to cash payments

technical.prompt: What is tokenisation in payments?

choices.answer: Replacing card numbers with tokens to protect data

technical.prompt: What is strong customer authentication or 3-D Secure?

choices.answer: Extra verification for online payments that cuts fraud

technical.prompt: What is an authorisation rate?
expectedPoints: Affected by fraud rules and data

choices.answer: The share of payment attempts that get approved
distractors: The rate at which merchants are licensed
The interest rate on credit cards

technical.prompt: What is a false decline?

choices.answer: A genuine payment wrongly rejected

technical.prompt: Why are cross-border card payments more expensive?

choices.answer: Higher fees, currency conversion and extra fraud risk
distractors: They are always cheaper than domestic

technical.prompt: What are local payment methods?
expectedPoints: Popular payment options in specific countries

choices.answer: Payment options popular in particular countries
distractors: Payments made only inside physical shops
Cash payments within a single town

technical.prompt: What is a digital wallet?
expectedPoints: Stores payment credentials on a device

choices.answer: An app storing payment details for quick checkout
distractors: A leather wallet with a chip
A bank account with no card

technical.prompt: Why do card rewards programmes depend on interchange?
expectedPoints: Regulation limits it in some places

choices.answer: Interchange income pays for card rewards
distractors: Rewards come from shop discounts only
Rewards have no cost to anyone

technical.prompt: What is surcharging?
expectedPoints: Merchant adds a fee for card payments
Rules vary by country and network

choices.answer: A merchant adding a fee for paying by card
distractors: A discount for using a card
A fee paid by the card network

technical.prompt: What is payment orchestration?

choices.answer: Routing payments across several providers from one integration
distractors: A musical performance at a bank
A single provider for all payments

technical.prompt: What does take rate mean for a payments company?
expectedPoints: Revenue as a share of payment volume

choices.answer: Revenue as a percentage of payment volume
distractors: The share of payments that are refunded
The number of payments per day
The rate at which customers sign up

technical.prompt: Why is debit card interchange often lower than credit card interchange?
A merchant on interchange-plus-plus pricing processes $200 million. Interchange averages 1.5%, scheme fees 0.1% and the acquirer's markup 0.3%. What does the acquirer earn?
A provider charges 2.9% plus 30 cents per transaction. What is the fee on a $50 sale?
A merchant attempts $1 billion of payments. Raising its authorisation rate from 90% to 92% adds how much approved volume?
expectedPoints: Small approval gains move large volumes

choices.answer: About $20 million

technical.prompt: A merchant's higher authorisation rate adds $20 million of approved payment volume. If the payments provider earns a 0.5% net take rate on that volume, what is the added revenue?
expectedPoints: Net take rate converts volume to revenue

technical.prompt: A merchant declines 5% of $100 million of attempted sales, and half of those declines were legitimate customers. How much genuine revenue is lost?
expectedPoints: Cost of overly strict fraud rules

choices.answer: About $2.5 million

technical.prompt: A provider charges a 2% FX markup on $10 million of cross-border payments. What does it earn from FX?
expectedPoints: FX markups are a key cross-border revenue

technical.prompt: A payments firm charges merchants 3% of volume but passes 2.2% to issuers and networks. What is its net take rate, and why does the distinction matter?

choices.answer: 0.8%; gross revenue overstates economics

technical.prompt: A payments company processes $50 billion at a 0.4% net take rate. What is its net revenue?
expectedPoints: Net take rate reflects what the firm keeps

choices.answer: About $200 million

technical.prompt: A merchant faces 100 chargebacks, each with a $25 fee and $60 of lost goods. What do they cost?

choices.answer: About $8,500

technical.prompt: How can network tokens improve authorisation rates?
expectedPoints: Card details update automatically when cards are reissued

choices.answer: Tokens stay valid when cards are reissued

technical.prompt: What is the trade-off in applying strong customer authentication to every online payment?

choices.answer: Less fraud, but more friction and abandoned checkouts
distractors: No effect on either fraud or conversion

technical.prompt: Why do global merchants offer local payment methods?

choices.answer: Customers prefer them, so conversion rises
distractors: Local methods are always more expensive

technical.prompt: How does payment orchestration help a large merchant?

choices.answer: Routing each payment to the best provider, with failover
distractors: Removing the need for any provider at all

technical.prompt: Why do regulators sometimes cap interchange?

choices.answer: To cut merchant costs where networks have power
distractors: To increase the value of card rewards
To raise the card issuers' profits

technical.prompt: Why do large merchants often pay lower processing fees than small ones?

choices.answer: They have volume and negotiating power
distractors: Fees are the same for all

technical.prompt: How do account-to-account payments differ from card payments for merchants?

choices.answer: They avoid interchange but offer fewer protections
distractors: They always cost merchants more than cards
They carry chargebacks just like cards

technical.prompt: What is friendly fraud?

choices.answer: A customer falsely disputing a genuine purchase
distractors: Fraud committed by a shop assistant
A fraud that causes no losses

technical.prompt: Why do merchants care about settlement timing?
expectedPoints: Some providers charge for instant payouts

choices.answer: Faster settlement improves their cash flow

technical.prompt: How can payment volume grow without new merchants?
A payments firm on blended pricing sees more premium credit cards used. What happens to its margins?

choices.answer: Margins shrink because costs rise while the blended price is fixed

choices.answer: Outages, pricing power and limited coverage
